title: Hospital passports, the digital flag and accessible information
blurb: Use hospital passports, the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag and the Accessible Information Standard so a person's needs follow them through every service.
question: Ellie, 35, has a severe learning disability and is admitted to an orthopaedic ward with a fractured wrist. Her support worker hands the nurse Ellie's hospital passport. What should the nurse do with it?

teach.h: Three tools, one aim: needs that travel with the person
teach.body: A hospital passport is a document the person owns, telling staff what they must know about them. The Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag is a national electronic marker showing the adjustments a disabled person needs. The Accessible Information Standard is the NHS and social care rule for identifying and meeting information and communication needs. In plain English: write the person's needs down once, share them properly, and use them every time.

rows.label: Who
values: NHS and adult social care users

head: Section
Examples
rows: Allergies, medicines, how I show pain, communication, capacity and consent
Routines, eating and drinking, personal care, who to contact
Music, foods, what calms me, what upsets me
teach.caption: Templates vary locally; the person owns it and it goes with them on admission.

teach.h: Scenario: Ellie arrives on the ward
teach.body: Ellie, 35, has a severe learning disability and a fractured wrist. The nurse reads her passport straight away: Ellie shows pain by rocking and biting her hand, takes an anti-seizure medicine at set times, and calms with her own music. The nurse uses it to plan pain assessment, medicines and communication, keeps it with Ellie where every shift can use it, checks the digital flag, and updates the passport with Ellie and her supporter before discharge.

The flag is a national, visible marker on a person's record, held on the National Care Records Service, showing the reasonable adjustments a disabled person needs. It is for any disabled person, not only people with a learning disability. Information standard DAPB4019 (December 2025) requires all NHS and publicly funded health and adult social care providers in England to share, read and write the flag fully by 30 September 2026. It is shared by implied consent; people can object.

steps.label: Identify
steps.sub: Ask about information and communication needs

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: The need itself, not just the diagnosis

steps.label: Flag
steps.sub: So it is visible whenever the record is used

steps.label: Share
steps.sub: With other services, as part of referral

steps.label: Meet
steps.sub: Easy read, BSL, longer time, a supporter

teach.caption: Applies to NHS and publicly funded adult social care, including carers and parents.

items.label: Kept with the person; used in handover
Updated and returned to the person

items: Write it with the person, in their words where possible, plus family and supporters.
Put the life-saving information first: allergies, medicines, pain, communication.
Check medicines against current records: a passport can go out of date.
Hand it back at discharge, updated with what was learned.

teach.text: A hospital passport belongs to the person: do not file it away in the medical notes. And do not confuse the tools: the AIS covers information and communication needs; the digital flag records reasonable adjustments of any kind for any disabled person; the passport is the person's own guide to them.

items: Hospital passport: person-held; must-know, important, likes and dislikes; travels with the person.
RADF: national marker of reasonable adjustments for any disabled person; full use by 30 Sep 2026.
AIS: identify, record, flag, share, meet, review.
Record the need (e.g. easy read), not just the diagnosis.
Read the passport on admission, use it every shift, update and return it at discharge.

summary: You can now use a hospital passport on admission and discharge, explain what the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag is and its 2026 deadline, and apply the Accessible Information Standard steps. You can also tell the three tools apart.

A.q: Sophie, a student nurse, hears that Callum, 27, who has a learning disability, has brought his hospital passport. She asks her mentor what it is. What is the best explanation?
options: A GP referral letter listing his diagnoses and tests
A legal document recording his best interests decisions
A person-held guide telling staff what they must know
An NHS record used to check his eligibility for care
A.why: A hospital passport is a document the person holds, setting out what staff must know (allergies, medicines, communication, pain), what is important and their likes and dislikes.

whyNot.0: A referral letter is written by a clinician for another clinician, not held by the person.
whyNot.1: It is not a legal record of best interests decisions.
whyNot.3: It does not decide eligibility for care.

A.q: Gareth, a learning disability liaison nurse, is training outpatient staff on the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag. Which description is accurate?
options: A national marker of a disabled person's adjustments
A paper alert card the person carries in a wallet
A list of people with LD kept by each GP practice
A hospital alert used to flag safeguarding concerns
A.why: The RADF is a national, visible marker on a person's record (National Care Records Service) showing the reasonable adjustments a disabled person needs.

whyNot.1: The flag is electronic and national, not a paper card.
whyNot.2: That describes the GP learning disability register.
whyNot.3: The flag records adjustments, not safeguarding concerns.

A.q: A clinic manager asks which steps make up the Accessible Information Standard. Which answer is correct?
options: Assess, plan, implement and evaluate the need
Presume, support, respect, decide and restrict
Prevent, protect, partner, empower and account
Identify, record, flag, share, meet and review
A.why: The AIS (DAPB1605) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet information and communication needs, with review added in the 2025 update.

whyNot.0: This is the nursing process, not the AIS.
whyNot.1: This loosely echoes Mental Capacity Act principles, not the AIS.
whyNot.2: This echoes safeguarding principles, not the AIS.

B.q: Ellie, 35, has a severe learning disability and is admitted with a fractured wrist. Her support worker hands the nurse Ellie's hospital passport. What should the nurse do?
options: File it in the medical notes for the doctors to read
Read it, use it to plan care and keep it with Ellie
Return it to the support worker to take home
Copy it and then send the original back to the GP
B.why: The passport should be read on admission, used to plan care and kept with Ellie so every staff member can use it.

whyNot.0: Filed away, it will not guide everyday care across shifts.
whyNot.2: Sending it home removes the information when it is needed most.
whyNot.3: The passport belongs to Ellie and stays with her, not the GP.

B.q: Rhys, 22, has a learning disability and is writing his hospital passport with his mother and community nurse. They want the first page to cover things staff must know. Which item belongs there?
options: His favourite football team
The music he likes to listen to
How he shows that he is in pain
The name of his college course
B.why: The 'must know' section holds safety-critical information such as allergies, medicines, communication and how the person shows pain.

whyNot.0: Likes belong in the likes and dislikes section.
whyNot.1: Music he enjoys helps, but it belongs with likes and dislikes.
whyNot.3: This is useful background, not must-know safety information.

B.q: A care home manager asks when providers must have fully implemented the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag in England. What is the correct answer?
options: By 30 September 2026
By 1 April 2025
By 31 March 2028
By 1 August 2016
B.why: Information standard DAPB4019 (December 2025) requires full implementation by all publicly funded health and adult social care providers by 30 September 2026.

whyNot.1: This date predates the December 2025 standard.
whyNot.2: This is not the deadline in DAPB4019.
whyNot.3: August 2016 is when the Accessible Information Standard came in, not the flag deadline.

C.q: Nia, 40, has a learning disability and is admitted with pneumonia. Her hospital passport lists an anti-seizure medicine her GP stopped six months ago. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give the medicine listed, as the passport is her record
Discard the passport, as it is clearly out of date
Ask her support worker which medicine to give tonight
Reconcile medicines with current records and update it with Nia
C.why: Passports can go out of date. Medicines must be reconciled against current records, and the passport updated with Nia and her supporters.

whyNot.0: Giving a stopped medicine could cause harm; the passport is not a prescription.
whyNot.1: The rest of the passport is still valuable; it should be updated, not discarded.
whyNot.2: Medicines should be confirmed against current clinical records, not memory alone.

C.q: Oliver, 52, has a learning disability and needs information in easy read with pictures; this is recorded and flagged on his hospital record. He is now being referred to a community physiotherapy service. Which AIS step must the referring nurse complete?
options: Ask Oliver to tell the physio team himself
Include his information needs in the referral
Wait for the physio team to identify his needs
Send the physio team a copy of his full notes
C.why: The AIS 'share' step requires a person's information and communication needs to be shared with other services as part of referral.

whyNot.0: This places the burden on Oliver instead of the service.
whyNot.2: Needs already identified must be shared, not rediscovered.
whyNot.3: Sharing the full notes is excessive and may not highlight his needs.

C.q: Femi, 30, is autistic with a learning disability and has capacity. He tells the liaison nurse he does not want his reasonable adjustments shared on the national flag. What is the correct position?
options: He may object; staff record it and usually respect it
He cannot object, because the flag is a legal requirement
His objection needs a court order to take effect
His family must agree before his objection is accepted
C.why: Flag information is shared by implied consent; people can object to sharing at any time, and the objection is respected unless there is a valid reason why it should be shared.

whyNot.1: Providers must implement the flag, but individuals can object to sharing.
whyNot.2: No court order is needed to object.
whyNot.3: As an adult with capacity, his objection does not need family agreement.

reteach.title: Who owns it, what it holds, where it goes
reteach.question: How do you remember the difference between the passport, the flag and the AIS?

blocks.body: The passport is owned by the person and holds what staff must know about them. The flag is a national electronic marker of their reasonable adjustments, for any disabled person. The AIS is the rule that services identify, record, flag, share, meet and review information and communication needs.

blocks.text: Return the passport, updated, at discharge. It belongs to the person.

explain.body: Person-held. Things you must know (allergies, medicines, communication, pain, consent), things that are important, likes and dislikes. No single national template.

test.q: Zara, 24, is being discharged after an appendicectomy. A nurse plans to keep her hospital passport in the notes 'in case she comes back'. What should happen?
options: Keep it in the notes for her next admission
Send it to her GP for safe keeping
Shred it as it may now be out of date
Return it to Zara, updated with what was learned
test.why: The passport belongs to the person and should go home with them, updated with anything learned during the stay.

whyNot.0: Keeping it means Zara cannot use it at other services.
whyNot.1: It is Zara's document, not the GP's.
whyNot.2: It should be updated, not destroyed.

explain.body: A national marker on the National Care Records Service showing reasonable adjustments for any disabled person. DAPB4019: full use by 30 September 2026. Shared by implied consent; people can object.

test.q: A nurse tells a colleague that the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag is 'just for people with a learning disability'. What is the correct response?
options: It is for any disabled person needing adjustments
It is for people with a learning disability or autism
It is for people who lack capacity about their care
It is for adults with a learning disability aged 18+
test.why: The flag is for any disabled person accessing publicly funded health and social care, not only people with a learning disability.

whyNot.1: The flag is not limited to learning disability and autism.
whyNot.2: Capacity is not the criterion; disability and a need for adjustments are.
whyNot.3: The flag is not limited to adults with a learning disability.

explain.body: Identify, record, flag, share, meet, review. Record the need itself (for example 'needs easy read with pictures'), not just the diagnosis. Covers carers and parents too.

test.q: Under the Accessible Information Standard, what should be recorded for a person with a learning disability?
options: The diagnosis of learning disability
Their IQ score from school records
Their specific communication need
The name of their social worker
test.why: The AIS requires the need itself (for example easy read, a supporter, longer time) to be recorded, not just a diagnosis.

whyNot.0: A diagnosis does not tell staff what to do differently.
whyNot.1: IQ scores are not what the AIS asks services to record.
whyNot.3: Contacts may be useful, but the AIS concerns communication needs.

explain.body: Before admission: share the passport and check the flag. On admission: read the passport, meet AIS needs. On discharge: update and return the passport and share needs with the next service.

test.q: Kai, 30, has a learning disability and is booked for a planned hip operation in four weeks. What is the best way to make sure the ward is ready with his adjustments?
options: Ask the ward to read his notes on the morning of surgery
Tell Kai to explain his needs to each nurse he meets
Share his passport with the LD liaison nurse to plan ahead
Book him into a side room and wait to see how he copes
test.why: Sharing the passport and planning with the hospital learning disability liaison nurse before admission lets adjustments be ready on arrival.

whyNot.0: Reading notes on the day leaves no time to plan.
whyNot.1: This puts the burden on Kai.
whyNot.3: A side room may help, but adjustments should be planned in advance.
